Our team met General Ratko Mladic mainly to ask him about the men who were put in there in the house -- in the white house, and he confirmed to us that those people would be taken as prisoners of war to be exchanged with the others that are on the BSA side -- on the BiH side. But mainly he also talked about the issue of the soldiers that had been killed in Bandera Triangle. So he was trying to tell us that there was serious war in the Bandera area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document as well, and then move on to the rest of the associated exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are -- one second, please. 4436, any objection against admission? Madam Registrar registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04436 becomes Exhibit P38, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Earlier, Mr. Stojanovic, when you suggested that the short report, 35 men in the house, was already in evidence perhaps under D18. It is not D18. It is part of a 75-page document for which the parties were invited to report what portions of it they would select and would have admitted into evidence. And I think we have now three pages -- well, at least three portions indicated by the Prosecution and ten portions indicated by the Defence. I think it is part of that, but it has not yet been assigned numbers. I think that we need the relevant portions to be uploaded into e-court so that finally they can be admitted and then will be included in that exhibit. Then we -- I'd like to move to what remains now as associated exhibits. I take them number by number. 14468, which was initially not on the associated exhibits but has been added to it, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, as far as the Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 044 -- then, Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 114468, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was talking about 04469.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 04469. 04469 then receives -- becomes Exhibit P39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is UNMO daily report, 17th of July, 1995, 2300 hours. Okay. It's now clear. It is 4469, and you said it is P39, and is admitted into evidence. Next one, 4471, also added to the associated exhibits, initially not being listed. Any objections? Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 04471 becomes Exhibit P40, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P40 is admitted into evidence. Then I move on. I skip all those who have meanwhile been admitted into evidence. The next one on my list is 4438. Any objections? UNPROFOR sitrep 5th of July to 6th of July. No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4438 becomes Exhibit P41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Next one is 4440, "UNMO Report Re: Food Situation Srebrenica," 8th of July. Any objections? No. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4440 becomes Exhibit P42, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 4441 is the next one. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4441 becomes Exhibit P43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next one, 4442. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4442 becomes Exhibit P44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is admitted. Next one, 4445. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4445 becomes Exhibit P45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. 4446. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4446 becomes Exhibit P46, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 4448, in the absence of objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4448 becomes Exhibit P47, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. Next one is 4449. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4449 becomes Exhibit P48, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Next one, 4450. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 44450 [sic] becomes Exhibit P49, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The next one on my list would be 4459. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4459 becomes Exhibit P50, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P50 is admitted. Next one, 4461. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4461 becomes Exhibit P51, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. The next one is 15737, "UNMO Report Re: Srebrenica" dated 13th of July, 0609 hours. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 15737 becomes Exhibit P52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the last one is the diary of the witness Kingori, dated March to July 1995. Any objections, Mr. -- no objections. Before we decide on admission of this one, it is a rather lengthy document. Madam Registrar, is there a typewritten version uploaded into e-court or perhaps I should ask Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you expect us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to decipher all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't. And in fact, I don't believe that it's necessary to tender it, so I won't tender that one in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Defence has used it as well I think or referred to it. Mr. Stojanovic, if the Prosecution does not tender it, although it was indicated as an associated exhibit, would that -- would that trigger any need for you to have the document or portions of it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I made reference to this document and the relevant pages are 13, 17, 23, and 24 in the B/C/S, and in English these are pages 7, 9, and 12 of those both-sided pages. If the Prosecution does not want to have this admitted, and I confronted all this with what the witness said in terms of what has been recorded or not, then, once again, with your permission - although we don't need the whole document - I would suggest that we admit only the relevant pages, page 7, 9, and 12 in English, so basically three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you would have to do is to, first of all, consult with the Prosecution whether for contextualisation the Prosecution would like to add any page if you tender some of the pages. Then all the pages thus selected should be uploaded as a D exhibit. And then you would tender it once this is done. We'll then hear from you and then we'll decide on admission, but preferably pages selected by both parties together. Mr. Vanderpuye, you're available for consultation, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is one document 4439 which may have been overlooked. I'm not sure if maybe it was admitted through another witness and that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4439, let me just have a look. 4439, as far as I'm aware, was admitted as D17.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I missed that. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you confirm that 4439 was admitted as D17?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, your --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D17 was 4392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we separately now deal with D -- no, with 4439. Apparently I made a mistake, Mr. Vanderpuye. I apologise for that. 4439, any objection? It is UNMO headquarters sector daily sitrep report dated 7th of July, 1995, 2000 hours. No objection. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4439 becomes Exhibit P53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P53 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, since the Chamber has no further questions for you, this -- unless there's any need, Mr. Stojanovic, whether the questions in re-examination, have they triggered any need for any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, not on the basis of the questions put by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Kingori, I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I would wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We did not strictly follow the one-hour rule. We take a break now and we'll resume at ten minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber made a few errors. 65 ter 4469, which we admitted as P39, was already admitted as D13. 65 ter 4471, which we admitted before the break as P40, was already admitted as D14. For these reasons, P39 and P40 are vacated hereby. Before the next witness will be called by the Prosecution, I would like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the next witness, Witness RM255, be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, earlier it was indicated that if the Defence would have no objection that you would present the evidence of the next witness, RM255, as a 92 ter witness. May I take it that -- is there agreement between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's my understanding there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see Mr. Stojanovic is nodding "yes." Any further matter to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Just to tell you that he - as you were aware - was originally scheduled as our first witness, so we took the unusual view that we would have him viva voce. Now that that's not possible and we're, out of efficiency and effectiveness, we think that this is the best way to go and with some hope that we may be able to finish our witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in view of the fact that the Defence has agreed to hear the evidence of this witness as a 92 ter witness, the Chamber allows the Prosecution to present this witness as a 92 ter witness. One question, perhaps. Mr. Lukic, last time when we were briefly discussing the map binder, you said your specialist was not in court. Are there any objections? If so, we would not hear them at this moment. If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are objections. So P3 remains for the time being as marked for identification. We'll hear your objections at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM255, because that's how we will call you during these proceedings. We'll not use your own name and please take care that -- in giving your answers that you do not reveal your identity either. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness RM255. Please be seated. Witness RM255, you'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We would first like to hand the witness the pseudonym sheet, 28116. It's a -- I think the best way to ensure that it's -- the screen is not shown to the audience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that you?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 65 ter number being - let me have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number, Madam Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P54, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P54 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And hello, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll begin by reading a short summary - it won't have everything you've always told us - and then I'll ask you some questions so we can go over your story.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In July 1995 the witness and his family lived in Srebrenica town. At that time, the conditions of life in the enclave were difficult. Sporadic humanitarian aid resulted in severe food shortages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On 11 July 1995, out of fear that they would be killed as a result of constant shelling, the witness and his family, together with the rest of the Muslim population, sought protection at UNPROFOR in Potocari. The witness's sons did not follow him to Potocari --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Instead --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't need to answer me at this point. This is just me reading, Witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The witness's sons did not follow him to Potocari. Instead, they left through the woods with the Muslim army. On the night of 11 July, the witness and his family had to spend the night in the open near the Dutch base along with thousands of others from Srebrenica. On 12 July Serb soldiers arrived in the area and came within the crowd of Muslims. The witness recalled VS soldiers providing bread and water to the people, which he felt was an attempt by the Serbs to hide their true intentions. That day buses and trucks arrived and people boarded them and went to Tuzla. He and his family were too far in the back to be able to leave that day. On the night of 12 July, the people were very frightened and he could hear screaming as Serb forces took people away. On 13 July the witness and his family approached the buses, but the witness was separated from his family and sent to a nearby house with other men from Srebrenica. He stayed in that house for about one hour and was then directed outside and put on a bus with other Muslim men and taken to a school in Bratunac. He and others were placed in a building where he stayed for two nights. During this time people were beaten and abused by military police and some people were taken from the building and never returned. They were not provided anything to eat, given only small amounts of water, and not allowed to use the toilet facilities. On the 15th, at about 1100 to 1200 hours, he and others were taken out and placed on buses and told they would be transported to Tuzla. During the drive the witness noticed they were not driving towards Tuzla but instead headed in the direction of Zvornik. They passed through Zvornik and came to a village he was later told was named Pilica, where he and the others were placed in a building that was either a school or a house of culture. That night Muslim men were taken outside by soldiers and he could hear sounds of beating and gun-fire and the process lasted through the night. The next day, the 16th, at around noon, he and some of the others had their hands tied behind their backs and were loaded onto buses and driven about 2 and a half kilometres to a large field, where he could hear gun-fire and was able to see bodies lying in lines on the ground. He and others were ordered off the bus and taken to the area where the bodies were and ordered to lie down by the soldiers, whereupon his group was cut down with gun-fire. He, however, was not injured and managed to untie his hands and eventually escape the area later that day. After several days, he and another survivor turned themselves into the Serb police and were taken to Bijeljina to a military prison. Finally on 23 December the witness was released. And, Mr. President, I would offer the -- I would, first of all, ask the witness if he was -- managed to last night look at a statement that he gave in May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it read to you last night?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know what this reading is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I explain to the witness. Witness, what Mr. McCloskey just read is a summary of what is in your statement. Since we'll not go through all of it, quite a lot of details may be missing. But for the public to be able to follow the proceedings, Mr. McCloskey just briefly summarised what is found in your statement. He now asks you whether yesterday you were able to read or have read to you the statement as you gave it at the time. Did I understand that you confirmed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, read it, all of it, this statement of mine, and all of it was fine. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked questions on those topics today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I'd say the same, and you can ask me whatever you want, I mean from that statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Every word is correct. No problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that exhibit, the 28330, the May 25th, 1996, statement to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 28330 becomes Exhibit P55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, McCloskey, I take it that you wanted to tender it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. We are currently working on a redacted version as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but the one to be admitted should be under seal. P55 is admitted into evidence under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we do have now a redacted public version, which is 28330.1, which we would also offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think - but I don't remember exactly - that is to be filed but not to be admitted in order to avoid that we have everything double in evidence. But we'll discuss that later. At this moment no decision will be taken on admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you remember how many times you've testified about this case here at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I was here five times. This is my sixth time, my sixth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay and -- now I'm going to ask you a few questions about the statement you gave, which the Judges have and have studied. So do your best to listen to my questions and we'll go forward. Can you tell us, your two sons that went through the woods with the army, about how old were they when they went through the woods with the army back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, one could have been about 23, he had just done his military service; and the other one, well, he was born in 1961, so he was 26, 27, I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what you have heard of the fate of your sons now?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, we just heard -- I mean, I guarantee this with my life, that they just went through the woods in order to protect their bare lives. I can guarantee that neither one of them had a rifle, neither one of them went into the woods with a rifle. They left as civilians. The younger one had been called out to dig trenches, whatever, and the other one had four children. He went to Zepa, brought food, so he could barely feed his children. The aid that arrived in Bratunac -- well, it would get there, you know, they would pick and choose whatever they wanted, and what was not for them, then that was sent on to Srebrenica. So we were really in a tough situation as far as food was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- okay. Have you buried your sons?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes. They found one of them somewhere in Kamenica and the other one was only 6 kilometres from crossing the line, that is, at Snagovo, above Zvornik, that's where they found his grave. I mean, they found the grave, but -- I mean, they even ground their dead bones, so not even all the bones are there. But I buried what was there. There are quite a few people who are in two or three graves. They were trying to hide this using machinery, going to different places in the woods and the mountains, trying to hide all of that. But people are being found. This year they buried 500, 520 of them. And then last year a bit over 5 00. And that's the way it is, every year they dig up these graves, they find them; others haven't been found yet. In this sad genocidal Srebrenica, that's where it happened. Many mothers and children suffer there and were buried and their remains --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: -- are being found to this day. I saw Mladic in Srebrenica then, I saw him. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM255, would you please carefully listen to the questions that Mr. McCloskey puts to you. And if he wants more information he'll ask for it. So please focus very much your answers on what Mr. McCloskey asks, and we have read your statement in detail. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Witness, I want to now take you to 13 July in Potocari that you talked about in your statement, and you say in that statement that on the 13th of July your family and you went towards the buses. Can you tell me who was with you in -- what was your family -- just which family members, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: My wife, my daughter, I was there, and then my grandchildren from my older son, and then when we left Potocari there was this roadblock and they would allow, say, only 200 people to pass there or 250 who were supposed to get to Tuzla by bus and that's how we passed that barricade. And then we got to this other one. Only 50 metres afterwards, there was this other barricade on the road and they were separating men from women and from children. And they said we just want to put a few questions and then we're going to let you go, and that's how it was. After one hour, that's how long we were there at that house, this Serb soldier came and said, Does anyone have any money? And one person said, I have about 100 marks. And he said, Hurry-up, until someone else comes in. So I wouldn't want to split it with them, so he just put it all in his own pocket, right. So then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. I'm sorry, but let me just go back a little bit. You mentioned that as you and your family went to the second barricade you were separated. Can you tell us who separated you from your family?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Karadzic's army, those who were down there. Karadzic knows that. He must have ordered that - that's for sure - to do that. Until Karadzic arrived -- the next day -- I mean, the next day Karadzic arrived in a van and that's when they started separating the men and then most of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I take it that you intervene at the right moment so to avoid that the Chamber has to do it again and again. And please keep the witness on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, as his -- the President has said, we need to try to stay specific to my questions, and that will be the best way to get through it. Remember, they have your statement and know the story. Where were you taken by the soldiers that separated you?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: They separated us in Potocari and it was the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: The primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't a clear question. Before you got to the area of the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, what place did they take you to in Potocari right after they separated you?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Then they separated us into a house and we spent an hour there, maybe, and then when the house was filled with men, say in an hour, they said, Come here to the bus. We sat down and it was off to Bratunac. We had to leave our bags outside, the little bit of food we had, and the rest, whatever. Then this primary school, that's where we spent another hour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: -- and then from there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I want to just go back to Potocari briefly. When you were in this house for an hour in Potocari, did anyone take your name down?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: No one was writing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did anyone interview you or ask you questions?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: No one over there. They were just asking for money. As for talks or negotiations, that could not succeed. A woman came there and she was just moaning, screaming, Genocide, genocide, don't go. Well, you have to go. When it's genocide, it's genocide. They go -- they take people out and they beat them, whatever, and it was basically troops do whatever you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Did you see any of the soldiers or anyone in this house where you were interview anyone or write down anybody's name?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any of that. I just told you about the man who was asking for 100 marks. And up there in Potocari, somebody was talking to IFOR and said Srebrenica is and showed this and then he said, Zepa, and then Gorazde, until the fall or the winter -- well, that's what I heard. And this other one said, There is this plane going around, just -- you can just see the lights, going around Srebrenica and then leaving. And then this other one said, Well, what do we need anybody for? Even America can do nothing to us. And he threw a hand-grenade, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remember to listen to my questions and we'll be through very quickly, but you will have a chance to tell further. I want to show you a picture that was shown to you the last time you were here, and it is 28083. If we could put that up on the screen. And I also showed this to you recently. Do you -- it should come up on your screen. And we need to blow that up. And if we look carefully at this, do you remember this photograph and marking on it in the last trial?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, this is Bratunac. This could be the primary school, and then from here where they took us to Vuk Karadzic, over here. Should I use a pencil to mark all of this for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, first, before we get to that, we can see - I hope you can see - that there are two small red marks on two different buildings in this photograph that you marked. Do you remember marking those in your last trial?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I do remember, but this could be the elementary school and the other one is the Vuk Karadzic school where we were transferred, this one here and that one here. I think this is the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: One of them definitely is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you see on one of the photographs it looks like there's a big black mark like the ceiling or the roof is caved in?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we cannot see what you are pointing at. Now, could I ask you, two buildings are marked. The one is a little bit further down, the other one is a little bit further up to the right. The one which is down and more to the left, what is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the elementary school, and this is the Vuk Karadzic. But they have renamed this school since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Vuk Karadzic school, is that the one a little bit higher up with a smaller red marking than the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the Vuk Karadzic school, the smaller of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we use the pointer on the screen so that we assist the witness in -- could you carefully look at where the arrow is at this moment. Could you tell us, is that the elementary school where the arrow is now? Can you see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the elementary school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and there is the road, and it is connected to this other school with a corridor or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We now move to the other school with a pointer, please follow the pointer. You see the other building now. Is that the Vuk Karadzic school? Perhaps if the pointer could be moved a bit so that the witness is better able ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that is the elementary school because the Vuk Karadzic is the bigger one. As well for this one, it's next to the road. So we entered this school building and after an hour we moved to this place where they were killing people day and night and taking them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. After having corrected himself, the witness now points at the building with a small red marking to the right and higher up as being the - let me now - the elementary school; and the building further down, a larger construction with a slightly red marking as the Vuk Karadzic school. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28083 becomes Exhibit P56, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P56 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I want to take you to the time right after you escape from the execution at this farm where you're able to untie your hands and you get into the woods. And did you meet some people in the woods that also escaped that you were not able to keep up with?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, another four men managed to escape and I was a fifth one. So when we came out it was dark, there was moonlight, and we went to the forest and it was pitch dark there. I was the oldest among them. They couldn't wait for me, so I was left alone behind. It seems that they had been captured on the way and they ended up in Zvornik, but nobody has ever heard or seen them. When I arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a question about that. When you were still with those four men, did you learn that any -- where any one of them was from, the village?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I asked one man and he said that he was from Jagodnja, but he never came. He's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any signs of injuries to any of these four men?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: One of them had bloody trousers, but I don't know whether it was from his wound or whether it was somebody else's blood. Since it was dark, I couldn't see whether he was limping or not, but I can say that I saw blood on his trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've described before and in your statement that at the execution site you remembered a fruit tree. And have you been back to that execution site in the last few years?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who took you back?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I was taken by a German crew and our crew as well, so I went twice. They videotaped the site and processed it, took pictures, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see that fruit tree that you spoke of in your 1996 statement?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this fruit tree, only it was bigger, and there's another one that has sprouted from it in this same location. And there's a grave nearby where people were executed, from which they later exhumed the bodies, dragged them somewhere in order to conceal them, so lots of bodies were crushed, their bones --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: -- were crushed and you can find one person in three graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now lastly, just yesterday do you recall telling the investigator and myself that you wanted to tell us something that you've never told us before? You mentioned you'd had a vision about General Mladic and you said something about him being at one of these places. Now, Witness, the Trial Chamber's not interested in visions, but what can you tell us for sure that you saw in relation to General Mladic and -- you need to make sure about this, it's important.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, when first people allegedly went to Sarajevo, I saw that they were not tied, their hands were free so that they could take out the money and pay, and then his army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we are not familiar with the term that the witness is using.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were doing the killing and the others were escorting the buses - I'm talking about the soldiers. So there were only a few of them left who were taking people to the bus. And then when he came, he brought with him 2 metres of white cloth, 2 metres of green cloth -- as I could see personally, that man was Mladic, only he was bareheaded and his shirt was unbuttoned and you could see his chest. And he was carrying those two pieces of cloth. And then there was a man accompanying him and he had an automatic rifle across his chest. He looked like to me exactly like Mladic only he didn't have the cap that he had in Potocari. This time he had no cap on his head. He gave those two pieces of cloth to two of our men, said, Tear it up into pieces and tie up your hands yourselves. And then he left. And later on three or four soldiers took us to the buses and one of them hit me with a rifle-butt. My hands were tied behind. I had to bend down. Nobody allowed us to look around, but I managed to see that up there in a shade there was this same man who gave me the cloth, and there were three or four of them all together, but that was Mladic as far as I could judge and as far as I knew him, only he didn't have a cap on his head. He was red in the face, bareheaded, with an automatic rifle. So it was him, no question about it, 100 per cent. And I didn't include this in my statement because I couldn't remember everything because I went to terrible fears and frights. And when the time came for me to make a statement was the time when I came out of the camp. And I can tell you, the 27 members of my family perished, including my two daughters-in-law, the men-folk from my family, and what can one do except lose one's mind? And on top of that, when I realised that my sons were missing, that my family was missing in the genocidal Srebrenica, I used to speak very honestly about everything, and I said that boys as young as 15 years were killed and even people over 60. These people are not required for military purposes. They even killed people up to 80 years of age --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: -- on the least -- on the year before last an 84-year-old man was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming here once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We have this new schedule with shorter hearings. Who will cross-examine the witness? Will it be Mr. Stojanovic? Mr. Stojanovic, one hour would be in the next ten minutes and we went on the first session a bit longer. Would it be a good idea that we take a break now and that you would cross-examine the witness after the break and how much time would you need for that? How much time would you need for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our estimate is that the cross-examination lasts one hour and we have now this new piece of information provided by the witness, so it seems that we shall need one hour and maybe it's best if we went on break now and then continue after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break now. But perhaps first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps one thing that may help. I just wanted to be able to tell the Court that it is not the Prosecution's intention to rely on this most recent evidence related to General Mladic or Karadzic. I wanted to bring that out so that you could see that. I think we've asked him -- perhaps too much of this witness, but we will not be relying on that. We rely on his statement and all the corroborating evidence in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, which of course if you said you would need one hour, would this change your position as to be in need of more than one hour? The Prosecution is not going to rely on the last portion which does not appear in the statement, that is, where the witness said that he recognised Mr. Mladic at a certain moment. So only on the statement, same for Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood Mr. McCloskey correctly, this portion of the evidence will not be admitted into evidence, then in that case I will conclude my cross-examination within an hour and I'm not going to address this issue. And there is a submission about Mr. Mladic's alibi on the relevant date and I wouldn't go into that matter at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to say not to admit, it is of course evidence given, but the Prosecution will not rely on it. So they'll not invoke that in support of their case. That's how I understand Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can reach a stipulation of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you speak with each other during the break. Mr. Stojanovic, if we would resume at five minutes past 1.00, we would have left 40 minutes. If it would be reasonably possible to finish the cross-examination in those 40 minutes, of course that would enable us to release the witness, to excuse him further. But of course if you really need his time -- the time you indicated, then we have to take a half an hour more tomorrow morning. But please try and see to what extent you could elicit the evidence in the time remaining in the last session. We'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it seems unlikely that we will be able to begin the evidence of the next witness, may I have the permission to release the Dutch interpreters and the witness for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be clear. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, when waiting, could you already give us an indication as to if you say you object to the admission of the map of -- the binder of maps? Is it specific maps or?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All those maps, Your Honours, have drawings, have facts inserted inside them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we wouldn't object if they were only maps, but obviously every single page is evidence that has to be led through the witness or introduced somehow, but we cannot agree still because we still don't know if the facts on the map are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any way to find out if, for example, if I saw some maps of a sniping incident, whether the victim was located at a certain place, is there any way that you would agree on that or try to agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it would ask for much more work we have to perform to be able to agree on the -- even on the locations of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we've heard your submissions. Then, Mr. Groome -- but is the witness escorted into the courtroom because that's our priority at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I could have an opportunity to speak with Mr. Lukic and then we could discuss whether there's a sensible way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then later hear from you. Mr. Lukic, that would also apply for maps of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps which are -- seem to look as army maps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Witness RM255. Witness, you'll be now cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Listen carefully to his questions and try to answer those questions. Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to put as clear as possible questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, if I understood you correctly, in 1995 you were not militarily engaged; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. My sons even didn't have any rifles, let alone me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The youngest son of yours that you mentioned here as having gone to dig trenches and fortifications, did he have military assignment in that year?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, he did have and I think I also had one, but I was not supposed to carry a rifle. I was just to stand guard and to warn people if it is necessary flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number because of the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, there was some overlap. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court document Exhibit 28066, according to 65 ter which shows a list of members of the Poznanovic company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, taking into account the measures that are in place --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am prepared to take due care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just hoping it's not being broadcast at this point. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document should not be broadcasted and you should have indicated that already spontaneously, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I was duly careful about this and I wanted to ask the witness without mentioning anything whatsoever, can -- to tell me just if he can see his son's name on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And of course you don't have to give me any details, numbers, et cetera. Just tell me if he is there or not?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I cannot read it from this distance. It is possible. He could have been on a list, but everyone has to defend oneself. A woman was killed while working the field and there was another person in civilian clothes as well. Two women were killed from an aircraft. What kind of aircraft were there? Who sent them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, let's keep it very practical. Did you want to bring to the attention of the witness the entry on the first page under number 4? Is that the one you would like him to look at specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. And we're only going to admit this into evidence, so I will not insist on this any further. We just have to go through the document so that I can establish a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then, apart from -- could the witness be shown the list so that he can read it and not to be shown to the public and then in his own language, so that is the B/C/S version of it. Could we enlarge entry number 4. Can you read the name there, Witness, under number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name of one of your sons and his year of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With your permission, we would like to tender into evidence this document marked under 65 ter Rule 28066 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I was not supposed to stand guard. I should have waited in my house to be killed and everything else? My whole family, my wife, my children -- so was I supposed to sit and wait in my house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no question was yet asked in this respect. Any objection, Mr. McCloskey? Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28066 becomes Exhibit D23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. D23 is admitted into evidence under seal. Mr. Stojanovic, I've not looked at the original, but I take it that sooner or later you'll explain to us through evidence the date of this list, because it refers to persons having joined on the 30th of April, 1992. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at one point on the 11th of July you decided, along with your family, to head for the UNPROFOR command in UNPROFOR, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who told you to go in that direction?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I saw that the army was leaving, going away, and IFOR who was there, they also withdrew, so everybody else had to go and move out. And despite the fact that my ancestors and I spent my whole life there, everything was damaged and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone specifically tell you to head for Potocari or was this your personal decision?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, the shells coming from Zeleni Jadar and Zvijezda, from Caus told us that because they were impacting cross-wise. So we were told that by the shells. And the shells do not discriminate between women, children, or whatever. You have to run because otherwise you won't survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, do you know who told your sons to leave through the forest together with the army?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, this was also told them by the shells as well as many civilians who had gone through the woods together with the army. Because the people knew what the Serb army was and they were killing everyone and swiping them and obliterating them like a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that was a decision made by anyone from either civilian or military authorities, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, definitely people headed off because they saw that Srebrenica was falling. There were thousands of mothers crying their eyes out and also children, and they are still crying to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you decided to go to Potocari and the men of military age towards the forest in Jaglic and Susnjar, you didn't see the Serb army anywhere in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I didn't, but I did see them in Potocari. I saw the Serb army who came later, there were shells falling around --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to Potocari, sir, later. We are still talking about Srebrenica and the 11th of July, and we can agree that at the time when you headed for Potocari there was no Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But Srebrenica was on fire. Shells were falling down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is, if I understood you correctly, after your arrival at Potocari you spent there two days in total, 11th and 12th, and then you were moved on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to hear from you is this: On the 13th, if I understand correctly your statement, you were separated and transferred to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I hear that you are already responding when Mr. Stojanovic is still asking his question. Interpreters cannot interpret two persons speaking at the same time. So please wait until the question is finished and then answer that question. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That first day, the 12th of July, you didn't see any separation of men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it on the 11th, but on the 12th I think that Mladic arrived and negotiations took place. There was a female who was shouting there, Genocide, genocide. They couldn't reach any agreement because Mladic wanted to kill a large number of people and let go the rest of them, but our people didn't agree to that and that's how Mladic acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that this was his intention, that he wanted to do that?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: What else? He was at the top of this policy, Karadzic, Milosevic, and himself. They are like three brothers, like triplets, they're all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, to the extent you wanted to establish that the basis of the knowledge of the intent of Mr. Mladic, that there may be no factual basis. If that would be your point, then it's clear to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally saw General Mladic in Potocari at any point?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When they were throwing loaves of bread in order to demonstrate how humane they are and when they were distributing chocolate to the children and all of that was videotaped, but they did not videotape how they committed genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Chamber if in this statement that was admitted into evidence that you gave back in 1996, you mentioned that you saw General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was in Potocari, definitely, 100 per cent. And only after he came the men were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you remember - and you said that this statement was read out to you again and that you stand by it in its entirety - in this statement given in 1996, did you ever mention seeing General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I mentioned it, he was there. I did not say in my statement that he was in Pilica. I was so shocked. I -- the number of people who were killed, my sons were killed, I myself -- it's a miracle that I survived all of that, the sheer fear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at this together. Your Honours, bearing in mind the last answer and the one before that, let us please view another video-clip, 1D00070. It has to do with footage of Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you nearby if you look at this footage now?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I managed to catch a loaf of bread myself. Yes, I was there and yes it was being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic at all during those moments?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, Mladic was there. He was walking around there and the loaves of bread were being thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far away was he?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, maybe 10 metres, and then down here the loaves of bread were being thrown out and this was being filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he wear a cap then?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon in his hands? Did he wear a cap then?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I've already told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon at his hands?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on his shoulder, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The buses that transported the population, at the moment when this bread was being distributed, had they already arrived?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Some people were eating earlier, others later, and then when the bus got there, then it went away. I mean, I wasn't watching the vehicles out there because they were lower down and then people would take their seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the buses arrived, people were shuffling and they wanted to get onto the buses as soon as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, yes, fear. They wanted to leave. It was a question of death and life and they wanted to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That first day you did not get onto the buses because you didn't want to be in that crowd?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: No, I left on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally did not see any of the killings that occurred on those two days in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I did not see that, but cries were heard, screams. When people would jump up in one area then everybody would jump up out of fear. Then we asked the Serb soldiers where was this, and they said a woman had a baby. And they were even laughing, they were making fun out of it. And that happened about ten times, these screams, this noise. And after that you just hear, say ten minutes later, either moaning or cries or -- and then you'd hear a rifle or an automatic rifle or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on with my questions. The next day, the 13th, when did you set out towards the buses, what time of day?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I set out perhaps at 9.00, and maybe I got to the bus only at 1.00 or 2.00. It was so crowded. People were pushing around and you couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there were two obstacles?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was one where the people were allowed to go through and the other one where they were being separated?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then this first obstacle or barrier, where they let the people go, do you remember that there were two UN APCs there and they were like a funnel and that is how people were allowed in?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, maybe. There were soldiers there that were also blocking the road. As I passed by, our hands were together like this and then they would let us go, and then they would actually hold their hands and they wouldn't let us get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 65 ter 1D00077. Your Honour, this is an aerial image of the area of Potocari, the 13th of July, and the time was roughly the one that was pointed out by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think the interpreters have difficulties hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we've overcome that now. I would just like us to zoom in on the central part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Can you recognise the road between Potocari and Srebrenica, or rather, between Bratunac and Srebrenica and the buses that can be seen in this image? Can you see all of this?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, if it's this road here ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind the fact that we are going to have a problem with identification, I shall go on. I'm not going to tender this into evidence because already tomorrow we will have an opportunity of having it admitted. However, may I just tender 65 ter 1D00070 and then I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, apparently tendered from the bar table. Is there any problem as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm apologising. It's the video we saw, the distribution of bread. Any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video number 1D00070 becomes Exhibit D24, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D24 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I wish to ask you is the following. You said that at one moment you received information to the effect that the people who were being separated would be questioned and then sent on to Tuzla. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, were you informed that there was a list of persons who were wanted for having committed war crimes and who were among these masses of people? Did you hear about any of that?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I did hear about that, but that was not investigated. I mean, you know, you take people to a camp and then you investigate there. You do not just kill everybody because they're Muslims, you know, you don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us please try to stick to the answers. I fully understand you and I have every possible respect for the tragedy that you experienced, and I express my full condolences on behalf of the Defence and General Mladic. But did you see the men being separated?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I didn't see the document but I saw them, who were separating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have 65 ter 17833 in e-court, please, and while we're waiting I wish to say that this is a document that is entitled: "List of Persons Who Are Wanted as War Crimes Suspects." And I shall quickly move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a man of 80 or 84 is not a war criminal. That would not be possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's wait and see what the question is. Please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question, sir: Did you ever in Potocari or in the school in Bratunac, did you ever see this list in the hands of the Serb soldiers? And I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, they did not bring out a list for me to read; that was their secret. They were doing one thing and saying another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender document 65 ter 17833.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I would object. I don't think this is the witness for this particular document. This is a genuine document. There are -- one of the people on our list is -- may be associated with this document, but I don't believe this witness, since he knows nothing about it, is really the person for this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If there's no objection in itself against the list to be admitted into evidence, then perhaps the parties could sit together and see under what rule they could have this admitted into evidence. But the witness says he had not seen a list although he heard about it and that seems not to be a very good basis for admission. But this is not an attempt to bar anything from being -- becoming in evidence. Would the parties agree to sit together and to discuss the matter how to introduce this list, either through another witness or by any other way? Then I'll not invite --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We shall certainly agree on this. I don't think there will be a problem. Let us deal with this in another one of our cross-examinations of another witness. So I withdraw my motion to have it admitted into evidence at this moment because we shall be going back to this document many times. May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, but please keep in mind that we have to finish in a couple of minutes. I do not know how much time you would still need more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, unfortunately I did not manage to finish within these 35 or 40 minutes. I think I need another 15 minutes or so. I have three more documents and a few more questions related to Pilica, Branjevo, and the process of separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although we looked for quite a number of minutes to video which seemed not much to add, that is, the distribution of bread about which the witness has testified, but let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if we would try to finish the evidence -- would you need time for re-examination as matters stand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, Madam Registrar is exploring whether it would be possible to continue for another 15 minutes. Again, we need the co-operation of many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes, Mr. Stojanovic, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll do our best to finalise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, these people who were involved in the separation, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: They had multi-coloured clothes, and those who were doing the separation, that was the Serb army. The ones manning the first barricade, I am not sure whether it was UNPROFOR or the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were members of the police or MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know. They all wore the same clothes. I didn't pay too much attention because I was terrified, so I just passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know whether those were members of the police or the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I think that they were military because they had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you familiar with these persons Nesib Mandzic, son of -- Camil, and Avdo Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know anyone called Nesib, but I heard of him. But I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the men or the person called Ibran Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know him either. But I know that this person has died. I think that at the time he was the president or the chief of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look now at document 1D00084, 65 ter. While we are waiting to have this document, this is a segment of pages 386 and 387 of the book entitled: "The Planned Chaos," written by Ibran Mustafic, who was in Potocari in those days and who describes the separation in the following manner. Can we have the next page, please. The last paragraph underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The author of this book says the following: "At that time, a check-point was set up on the little bridge across the Rabin creek manned by Chetniks, several soldiers of the Dutch Battalion, Nesib Mandzic, Ibro Nuhanovic, and Camil, and they were letting people through and separating them. I knew that they had been in Bratunac negotiating, but I could not believe that I was seeing with my own eyes that several Dutch soldiers, Nesib, Ibro, and Camil were working together with the Chetniks on separating people." I'm asking you, do you remember that somebody from Srebrenica whom you knew and in the presence of the Dutch soldier pointed out to people who should be singled out from the column?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know. And as for Mustafic who wrote this, he must have written it under duress because he had been in a camp and he must have written it as they dictated it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start interpreting or speculating on the book, the witness said that he didn't know any of these persons. Now apparently you are putting to him what is a description of the role of those persons, and then you asked the witness whether you remember that someone from Srebrenica - whom you knew and in the presence of the Dutch soldiers - which seems to be a clear reference to the persons you mentioned, of which the witness said he doesn't know them. So therefore I wonder whether you could put a question to the witness which he can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm not going to deal with this document any longer. I will tender it through another witness because we shall have to deal with this matter extensively in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you a few more questions. Can you recall how many buses set off from Bratunac towards Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone driven from the school in Bratunac before you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know if they were taken somewhere further, I don't know, but I do know that on that side there were killings going on during day and during night because people were screaming, there were shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you boarded these seven buses, were any people left behind in the school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I don't think so. There were seven buses and I think that everybody boarded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the school or the centre in Pilica, did you from those seven buses enter the school first?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone. When we entered Pilica there was -- the bus stood there for about two hours. I don't know what they did with the people living there, but they knew that there was going to be killing and shooting. I didn't see anyone because it was already dark. When we were driven there, there were four pillars in front of the door and I hit one of those pillars because it was too dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me how many people were on the bus that you were on, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, about 50 people, according to the number of seats, and they were mainly all full.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were all those people from the seven buses put up in the centre in Pilica or the school in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were driven towards Branjevo on the following day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I think that we spent there two nights and one day, and on the third day, whether it was the 16th or the 17th, people were taken out to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did they drive you until you came to a place where the buses stopped?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I cannot tell you that, but I think between 2 and a half and 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many buses took you from the school to that location?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: As far as I know, two buses in each batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between the place where the bus stopped and the location of the execution, can you tell us how long you walked?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I would say between 60 and 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, interpreters and transcribers need time, so do not -- take a very little pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How big were the groups of people taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Between 20 and 25 or 27, so 50 people in two batches were taken out and shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your evidence, there was a total of eight to ten soldiers. Do you still stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Inasmuch as you were able to estimate, how many groups were needed to vacate or empty a bus?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, two groups were taken out and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You described to us how you managed to survive, but I'm asking you this: Whilst you were still in the place where you fell onto the ground, were you able to estimate the time that elapsed until the next buses arrived?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, it's 2 and a half kilometres, up to 3 kilometres, as I said, so they came and left immediately. And then they came and left immediately. So they were shooting people next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point after you were wandering around this area you decided to give yourself up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you appeared before some policemen that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, there were two policemen and a driver when we surrendered ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were transferred to the military command in Karakaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, but they just dropped by in a restaurant owned by a good Serb who gave us food, who gave us drink, who gave us a pack of cigarettes each, and all credit due to him because he was a real good man and I kissed him and I started crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after you reported to the military command, you and a group of other people of Srebrenica were transferred to Batkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as you arrived at the Batkovici camp, you were recorded by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct and that is how it happened. They registered us immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were never abused, harassed, or beaten in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Well, I personally wasn't, but some people were though. But as far as I'm concerned, I did not report anything to anyone. That's how I survived. But I wasn't beaten, I wasn't maltreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I said I would be strict. You've one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Five months later you were exchanged in Batkovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, we go back to the 13th. On the 13th of July, when you were separated in Potocari, did you at any point see General Mladic there?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I only saw him when those loaves of bread were thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you recall -- you said that he had a rifle. Did he have it in his hand or over his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: He had an automatic rifle over his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I don't know how knowledgeable you are about the weapons, but was that the rifle called Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: I'm not very knowledgeable about the weapons, but I do know that that was an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I really am sorry if I forced you to re-live all these terrible events that you had to go through.

utterances.speaker: RM255
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding, but whatever anyone deserves that should come their way. There are good Serbs. I have always maintained that. But their command was such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I would first like to hear from Mr. McCloskey whether there are any questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM255, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague. As it was said before, it's not the first time and it's a long journey for you. We appreciate that you came and that you've answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And you may -- you are excused and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank you for inviting me to tell the truth here and to seek justice. And there can be no justice without life sentence. Many, many tears have been shed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we are not at a point that we would discuss sentencing. Please follow the usher and have a safe trip return home again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day. I would like to thank all those who have assisted us even beyond the time apparently in full understanding of the urgency of concluding the testimony of this witness if possible today. We will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 20th of July, at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of July, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
